newsitem.title: USA: Clinton to renew MFN for China - officials.
newsitem.headline: Clinton to renew MFN for China - officials.

text.p: President Bill Clinton, firing the opening shot in what is expected to be a new foreign policy battle with Congress, will renew most favoured nation trade status for China on Monday, U.S. officials said.
"The president is going to announce MFN today," one administration official told Reuters.
Renewing favourable trade benefits for China "is very much in the national interest, and we will push very hard for it on the Hill (with Congress) and with (American) public opinion," he added.
Clinton will announce MFN renewal at 2:15 p.m. EDT (1815 GMT), officials said.
They said Secretary of State Madeleine Albright would also make the case for the administration position during an appearance on Monday in Delaware.
The president is required to make the decision annually by June 3.
Favourable trade benefits for China are controversial, and some members of Congress have already made clear their intention to try to overturn the decision.
Clinton, who has agreed to a summit with Chinese President Jiang Zemin later this year, has worked hard to improve ties with Beijing over the past two years.
But China's human rights record, its sale of missiles and technology to regions that are becoming destabilised and its huge trade surplus with the United States remain major problems.

Many in the United States -- including administration officials, lawmakers and businessmen -- are also concerned about the future of Hong Kong when control of the British colony reverts to Beijing on July 1.

Some lawmakers have suggested MFN be delayed or be renewed for a shorter time, such as three months or so, until they can see how China handles Hong Kong. Critics say Beijing has already begun to erode political rights there.
Administration officials and private analysts are reasonably confident Clinton can prevent his opponents from mustering the votes needed to override his MFN decision.

But few doubt the battle will be a bruising one. Clinton and his top aides had a hard time recently securing another of their key foreign policy goals of 1997: Senate ratification of the Chemical Weapons Convention.

Business leaders have been rallying commercial forces across the country since January to lobby lawmakers for renewal of the preferential trade status, which is given almost every country in the world. Only a handful of countries are denied MFN.
Supporters of normal trade relations with China had hoped to end the annual ritual and pass legislation this year to grant Beijing permanent MFN.

But strong opposition from social conservatives and liberal labour groups faulting China's human rights record, plus a scandal over alleged Chinese attempts to influence U.S. elections through illegal campaign donations, persuaded administration officials as early as February that permanent MFN was out of the question for now.

The United States' trade deficit with China was $7 billion in the first two months of the year, according to U.S. government figures, $2 billion higher than last year. It is the second-highest deficit after Japan's, which it is threatening to overtake.
